assessment_summary:
The statement is false. A standard counterexample is the Sierpinski space. Let X = {0, 1} with the topology {∅, {1}, {0, 1}}. The closed sets are ∅, {0}, and {0, 1}.

The space is normal because it contains no two non-empty disjoint closed sets. The only disjoint pairs of closed sets involve the empty set (e.g., ∅ and {0}), which can trivially be enclosed in the disjoint open sets ∅ and X.

However, the space is not regular. Consider the closed set C = {0} and the point x = 1, which is not in C. The only open set containing C is X = {0, 1}. Any open set containing x must be either {1} or {0, 1}. Neither of these is disjoint from X, meaning that x and C cannot be separated by disjoint open sets.
counterexample: X = {0, 1} with topology {∅, {1}, {0, 1}}. Closed sets are ∅, {0}, {0, 1}. Normal since no two non-empty disjoint closed sets exist, but not regular because point 1 and closed set {0} cannot be separated by disjoint open sets (the only open set containing {0} is X).
